lines.say: A box hides a secret string of bits, like one zero one. How many questions will it take?
Picture a wall of three switches, some secretly wired to a buzzer.
The buzzer only tells you if an odd or even number of wired switches are on.
Test them one at a time, and three switches take three questions.
A quantum computer needs just one question.
Each switch gets a qubit, a quantum bit, starting at zero.
A step called an H gate makes it plus, an even blend of zero and one.
An extra buzzer qubit is set to minus, the same blend with a minus sign. Then we ask once.
Each wired switch kicks a minus sign back onto its own qubit, turning plus into minus.
That sign is called a phase, so this is phase kickback.
Measure now, and plus and minus both give fifty fifty. The secret hides in the signs.
One more H on each qubit turns plus back into zero, and minus into one.
Measure, and we read one zero one, every time, from a single question.
But the computer didn't secretly try every setting and collect the answers.
It asked once, and interference, where possibilities add or cancel like ripples, left only the secret.
Here's where the switch wall breaks. A real switch is only on or off, never plus.
It only works for an odd or even rule, which interference can unpick. Most rules aren't.
That's Bernstein Vazirani: phase kickback on every input at once, so one question reveals the whole secret string.
